body: In September 2023, Sound Development Group LLC proposed a commercial and residential project in Oak Harbor on land next to Hal Ramaley Memorial Park: a one-story brewpub with single-story residential units. The city rejected that plan and encouraged a proposal with more urban density for downtown. The developer came back with a four-story Home2 Suites by Hilton with 107 rooms and meeting space. Its parking lot would extend onto part of the park.

At the time, the city code required voters to approve any sale of developed park property. According to the opinion, city planning staff gave the developer several options: hold an election, drop the fourth floor, cut the pool and other amenities to free up parking, or amend the code. The developer pursued the amendment. At an August 13, 2024 public hearing, the city council passed Ordinance 1999 by a six-to-one vote. It allows park property to be sold or traded without a vote if the council approves a development agreement and finds that the exchange meets set land-area and market-value tests, or that the private party's park improvements are worth at least 150 percent of the land conveyed. The city's planner told the council the change was prompted by the hotel proposal.

Whidbey Environmental Action Network sued on August 30, 2024. It argued the city violated SEPA by passing the ordinance without first reviewing its environmental impacts. The trial court granted summary judgment to the city on May 1, 2025, ruling that the ordinance was not an action covered by SEPA and was categorically exempt in any event, and dismissed the suit with prejudice.

Division One reversed in an unpublished opinion. Writing for the panel, Acting Chief Judge Bowman held that Ordinance 1999 is a nonproject action under WAC 197-11-704(2)(b)(i). Its conditions tie the transfer of park land to a specific purpose, development, and so they control the use or modification of the environment, much as a zoning ordinance does. The court rejected the city's position that review could wait until a sale or development was actually proposed. It noted that a concrete proposal already existed, with site plans, floor plans, landscaping plans and renderings showing the parking lot, and that accommodating the project was the city's motivation for the ordinance. The court also held that the procedural-action exemption in WAC 197-11-800(19) does not apply, because the ordinance contains substantive standards. The case goes back to the trial court for further proceedings.

timeline.label: Sound Development submits initial brewpub and residential proposal
Trial court grants summary judgment to city
Court of Appeals reverses and remands (unpublished)
